messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Train Conductor
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 43

As a train conductor for the past six years, Amir takes pride in his punctuality and his ability to read the subtle rhythms of the rail yard. His job requires a steady hand and an even steadier mind, a constant vigilance for the unexpected. Before the incident, he would describe his work as a kind of meditation—the rhythmic clatter of the wheels, the familiar announcements over the PA system, the quiet hum of the cabin. Now, that same environment has become a landscape of dread.

The event happened on a Tuesday afternoon, three months ago. Amir’s train was approaching a level crossing in a suburban area, the barriers down, lights flashing. He saw a car stopped on the tracks, just beyond the barrier. It was a silver sedan, an older model. He saw the driver, a woman in her forties, her face a mask of panic as she tried to restart the engine. Amir did everything by the book—the emergency brake, the long, piercing blast of the horn. But the train’s momentum was a physical law he could not break. The impact was a deafening, sickening crunch of metal. The train shuddered violently, and then there was silence, broken only by the hiss of the brakes and the ringing in his own ears.

He didn’t see the woman’s body. He was told later that she had been killed instantly. But what he sees, every single night, is the look on her face. It’s not a static image but a moving picture that plays behind his eyelids. The way her eyes widened, the frantic, useless turning of the steering wheel, the silent scream he imagines she let out. The sound of the horn, which he used to think of as a simple warning, now feels like a scream of his own, trapped in his throat.

Amir has been on medical leave for two months. He can’t bring himself to go back. The thought of stepping into the cabin, of feeling the familiar vibrations under his feet, makes his stomach clench into a knot. He starts to sweat just driving past the train station. He has nightmares three or four times a week, always the same. He’s in the cabin, but the controls don’t work. The horn is stuck, a continuous, wailing sound. He tries to look away from the car, but his head is locked in place, forced to watch. He wakes up gasping, his heart hammering against his ribs, convinced he can still feel the train shaking.

To cope, he has developed a series of rigid routines. He checks the locks on his apartment door three times before he can sleep. He will only eat food that is beige or white in color—pasta, rice, plain chicken. He avoids any news reports about car accidents or trains. He has stopped driving altogether, taking the bus or walking everywhere. The sudden sound of a car horn, even a distant one, makes him flinch and duck his head. He feels a constant, low-grade irritability, snapping at his mother when she calls to check on him, then feeling a wave of guilt that makes him feel even worse.

He used to be an easygoing man who enjoyed playing cards with his cousins on the weekend. Now, he avoids them. He feels like a different person, a ghost haunting his own life. He spends most of his days in his apartment, staring at the television without seeing it, or pacing from the kitchen to the living room. He feels a profound sense of shame, a conviction that he should have been able to stop the train, that he should have done something different. He knows, logically, that he followed every safety protocol, but the logic doesn’t touch the feeling. It’s a heavy, cold stone in his chest. He is tired, so deeply tired, but sleep offers no rest.
